summary: Defines S/MIME version 4.0, a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Digital signatures give authentication, integrity, and proof of origin, encryption gives confidentiality, and compression can reduce size. It obsoletes RFC 5751 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to put a signed, sealed envelope around an email so you know who sent it and nobody else can read it.

subtitle: How to sign, encrypt and compress MIME messages so email can be authenticated and kept private.

tldr.problem: Ordinary MIME email can be read and altered in transit, and the recipient cannot prove who sent it. Earlier S/MIME versions also relied on algorithms that had aged.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME prepares a canonical MIME entity, wraps it in a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) object (SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData or CompressedData), and carries that in application/pkcs7-mime or in a multipart/signed message with a detached application/pkcs7-signature.
tldr.outcome: Version 4.0 adds authenticated encryption (AuthEnvelopedData), AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, ECDSA and EdDSA, and adds SHA-512 while treating SHA-1 as historic. It obsoletes RFC 5751 and is itself updated by RFC 9788.

today: RFC 8551 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5751 (S/MIME 3.2). It has been updated by RFC 9788, which concerns protecting email headers.

sections.title: What S/MIME Provides
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) is a consistent way to send and receive secure MIME data. Using digital signatures it provides authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin; using encryption it provides data confidentiality. As a supplementary service it provides message compression.

It is not limited to mail. It can be used with any transport that carries MIME data, such as HTTP or SIP, and by automated agents, for example for signing software-generated documents or encrypting FAX messages sent over the Internet.

The specification builds a MIME body part that is cryptographically enhanced according to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), and defines the application/pkcs7-mime media type to carry it. It also uses multipart/signed with application/pkcs7-signature for detached signatures. Requirements are stated separately for sending agents and receiving agents, following the Robustness Principle: be liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME is a set of rules for putting a lock and a signature on a message. Anything that can carry a message, not only email, can use it.

sections.title: Algorithms and CMS Options
sections.content:
This RFC adds levels to the usual requirement words: SHOULD+ (expected to become a MUST later), SHOULD- (expected to become a MAY) and MUST- (a MUST that is expected to loosen).

  • Digest: agents MUST support SHA-256 and SHA-512.
  • Signatures, receiving: MUST support ECDSA with curve P-256 and SHA-256, and EdDSA with curve25519 (PureEdDSA); MUST- support RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 with SHA-256; SHOULD support RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256. Sending agents MUST support at least one of ECDSA P-256 or EdDSA.
  • Key encryption: MUST support ECDH ephemeral-static for P-256 and for X25519 with HKDF-256; MUST- support RSA encryption; SHOULD+ support RSAES-OAEP.
  • Content encryption: MUST support AES-128 GCM and AES-256 GCM; MUST- support AES-128 CBC; SHOULD+ support ChaCha20-Poly1305.

With ECDH, the key wrap and content-encryption algorithms must use the same key size. Of the CMS content types, only Data, SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData and CompressedData are used by S/MIME. Signers SHOULD include signed attributes such as signing time, SMIMECapabilities (a preference-ordered list of what the sender can handle) and an encryption key preference.

When a sender knows the recipient's capabilities, it SHOULD pick the first one in the recipient's list that it can use. With no knowledge of the recipient, it SHOULD use AES-256 GCM, and otherwise AES-128 CBC.
sections.plainLanguage: Before locking a message, the sender checks which kinds of locks the receiver knows. If it has no idea, it picks the strongest lock that everyone modern should have.

sections.title: Building S/MIME Messages
sections.content:
The data to be secured is always a canonical MIME entity. Preparation has three steps: prepare the entity locally, convert its leaf parts to canonical form, and apply appropriate transfer encoding. Text entities MUST use <CR><LF> line endings. A client that wants to protect headers such as Subject, To and From MAY wrap a full message in message/rfc822.

There are four ways to make a secured message, all using application/pkcs7-mime except the clear-signed form:

  • Enveloped: smime-type=enveloped-data. This gives confidentiality but no integrity protection.
  • Authenticated enveloped: smime-type=authEnveloped-data. This gives confidentiality and integrity, but not proof of origin.
  • Signed with SignedData: smime-type=signed-data. Recipients need S/MIME software to read it, but benign intermediaries cannot break it by rewrapping lines.
  • Clear-signed: multipart/signed, whose first part is the content and whose second part is a detached application/pkcs7-signature. It can be viewed with or without S/MIME software and is generally preferred for sending.

Compressed messages use smime-type=compressed-data, and a certificate-only message uses certs-only. A multipart/signed message has two required parameters: protocol (which MUST be application/pkcs7-signature) and micalg, naming the digest algorithm, for example sha-256.

These forms can be nested, and an implementation MUST be able to process arbitrarily nested S/MIME within reasonable resource limits. Signing first hides the signer inside the envelope; enveloping first leaves signatures verifiable without a private key.
sections.plainLanguage: You can seal the letter, sign it, or both. A signature written on the outside of a clear envelope lets anyone read the letter but still lets them check who wrote it.

sections.title: Media Types and File Extensions
sections.content:
Because CMS objects are binary, base64 transfer encoding is usually appropriate for the outer entity, especially over SMTP. Senders SHOULD include the smime-type parameter so a mail client can tell what is inside without decoding the ASN.1. They SHOULD also emit a name parameter and a Content-Disposition filename with an appropriate extension.

The extensions are .p7m (SignedData, EnvelopedData or AuthEnvelopedData), .p7c (certificate-only), .p7z (CompressedData) and .p7s (the detached signature). An implementation MUST use the media types and MUST NOT rely on file extensions, which only help when a gateway turns an unknown entity into application/octet-stream.

A message counts as S/MIME if it is application/pkcs7-mime, or multipart/signed with protocol application/pkcs7-signature, or application/octet-stream with one of the file suffixes p7m, p7s, p7c or p7z.
sections.plainLanguage: The file name ending is a sticker on the envelope that says what kind of seal is inside. The sticker helps, but the real label is the type written on the envelope.

sections.title: Certificates and Key Sizes
sections.content:
Certificate validation is covered elsewhere (RFC 5750); this RFC deals with what agents do once a certificate has been validated or rejected. A receiving agent MUST provide some way to retrieve certificates for recipients, and agents SHOULD let users store and protect correspondents' certificates.

All key pairs MUST come from a good source of non-deterministic random input, and the private key MUST be protected. An S/MIME user agent MUST NOT generate RSA signature keys smaller than 2048 bits. For RSA signing, 2048 to 4096 bits is a SHOULD, and keys of 2047 bits or less are SHOULD NOT. For verification, 2048 to 4096 bits is a MUST. Key sizes for ECDSA, EdDSA and ECDH are fixed by the curve.

S/MIME v4.0 does not require any particular certificate request mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks need good keys. Keys must be made with real randomness and be big enough that nobody can guess them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Algorithms weaken over time, so implementers need to keep checking that the ones listed still provide the expected security. The choice of 2048 bits for RSA is based on providing at least 100 bits of security. RSA and DSA keys under 2048 bits are considered by many experts to be insecure; an implementation that verifies signatures made with RSA or DSA keys under 1024 bits MUST warn the user. Algorithms such as RC2 offer little security over plaintext.

Sending the same message with strong and weak cryptography lets an observer decrypt the weak copy and learn the strong one, so a sender SHOULD NOT send a copy using weaker cryptography than it would use for the original. Unauthenticated EnvelopedData can be modified without detection, which is one reason for the move to AuthEnvelopedData.

Authenticated encryption alone does not prove who sent a message. The starting key must be bound to a single entity, there must be exactly one sender and one recipient, and a direct path must exist from the starting key to the content-encryption key. S/MIME's ephemeral-static key agreement and key wrapping do not meet these conditions. Even when they are met, the sender cannot prove origin to a third party, because either party could have created the message.

Appendix B advises that user agents treat signatures on historic mail differently, since CRLs may no longer be available and old keys and hashes may be weak.
sections.plainLanguage: Strong locks are useless if you also mail a copy sealed with a flimsy one. And a lock that two people share cannot prove which of them wrote the note.
